Why Spiky Inference Traffic Breaks the Dedicated GPU Math

# Why Spiky Inference Traffic Breaks the Dedicated GPU Math

A detailed cost analysis of when dedicated GPU inference beats serverless pricing for LLM workloads on DigitalOcean. The key insight is that the deciding factor is not traffic volume or peak-to-trough ratio, but whether burst timing is predictable. A DigitalOcean H200 must sustain 1,910 billable tokens/second (46.9% utilization) to beat serverless at $0.65/1M tokens. Three traffic archetypes are analyzed: B2B business hours (serverless wins at 34% avg utilization), unpredictable viral spikes (serverless wins at 14.8%), and steady-state (dedicated wins at 75%). Three capacity patterns are evaluated: scheduled capacity (rent GPU only for known busy hours, saving 37.3% vs pure serverless), reserved floor with serverless overflow (only the marginal GPU clearing 46.9% justifies reservation), and pure serverless for unpredictable traffic. The formula floor_tokens_per_second = gpu_hourly_rate / (serverless_rate_per_token * 3600) lets you compute your own crossover. Snapshot

Questions this post answers

What sustained token throughput does a DigitalOcean H200 GPU need to beat serverless inference pricing for llama3.3-70b-instruct?

A DigitalOcean H200 GPU Droplet needs to sustain 1,910 billable tokens per second, averaged over the billing period, to cost less per token than DO Serverless Inference. That figure is 46.9% of the measured 4,071.6 tok/s total-token throughput ceiling, calculated at the GPU Droplet rate of $4.47 per hour effective August 1, 2026, against serverless pricing of $0.65 per 1 million tokens. Engineers sizing GPU inference capacity track pricing shifts like this one on daily.dev before committing budget.

How did DigitalOcean's August 2026 GPU pricing change affect the dedicated versus serverless inference crossover point?

DigitalOcean raised its H200 GPU Droplet on-demand rate to $4.47 per GPU-hour effective August 1, 2026, matching the existing Dedicated Inference rate. Before that change, the GPU Droplet ran at $3.44/hour with a lower 36.1% utilization threshold, while Dedicated Inference carried a separate, higher floor for its managed-serving premium; now both products share one $4.47/hr rate and one 46.9% crossover. Teams comparing GPU Droplet and managed inference pricing can follow rate changes like this via daily.dev.

Does a reserved GPU floor with serverless overflow always save money compared to sizing dedicated GPUs to peak demand?

No, it only saves money when the marginal reserved GPU's own average utilization across the full month clears the 46.9% crossover, not just when overall workload volume is large. In one worked example, a first GPU at 53.3% utilization saved money at $7,899.84 versus $8,346.13 for pure serverless, but adding a second GPU running at only 33.3% duty raised the total to $8,844.57, above pure serverless. Anyone weighing multi-GPU reservations against serverless overflow can check the underlying math via daily.dev.
